extracted.intended_audience: students of mathematical logic (advanced undergraduate / beginning graduate)
extracted.subtask_description: Formal definitions, theorems, and constructive methods in sentential (propositional) logic: Boolean functions, connectives completeness, normal forms, switching-circuit cost/delay, compactness, and basic computability/decidability notions. The page presents standards and constructive procedures used to evaluate or produce formulas and circuits.

rubrics_metrics.name: k-place Boolean function
rubrics_metrics.description: A k-place Boolean function is a function from {F, T}^k into {F, T}. (A Boolean function is then anything which is a k-place Boolean function for some k. We stretch this slightly by permitting F and T themselves to be 0-place Boolean functions.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the basic object corresponding to connectives; sample Boolean functions (identity, negation, conjunction, disjunction, conditional, biconditional, constants) are given by explicit equations. Treat 0-ary functions as the constant truth-values ⊥ and ⊤.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extract Boolean function from a wff (Bα)
rubrics_metrics.description: From a wff α whose sentence symbols are among A1,...,An define the n-place Boolean function Bn_α by Bn_α(X1,...,Xn) = the truth value given to α when A1,...,An are given the values X1,...,Xn (i.e., v(α) where v(Ai)=Xi).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationally construct Bα by listing the 2^n truth assignments and recording α's truth value for each; truth tables (example Table V) instantiate this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entailment via Boolean functions (Theorem 15A (a))
rubrics_metrics.description: α |= β iff for all X ∈ {F, T}^n, Bα(X) ≤ Bβ(X) (with F < T).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently: whenever v(α)=T then v(β)=T for each assignment v. Use pointwise order F < T to check entailment by comparing Boolean functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tautological equivalence criterion (Theorem 15A (b))
rubrics_metrics.description: α |==| β iff Bα = Bβ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two formulas are tautologically equivalent exactly when they define the same Boolean function (i.e., same truth table).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tautology criterion (Theorem 15A (c))
rubrics_metrics.description: ⊨ α iff Bα is the constant function with value T.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A formula is a tautology precisely when its Boolean function is identically T on every assignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realizability of Boolean functions by wffs (Post's theorem, Theorem 15B)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any n-place Boolean function G (n ≥ 1) there exists a wff α such that G = Bn_α.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct α by listing all input tuples where G= T, for each such tuple form a conjunction of literals (xi or ¬xi) that matches it, and disjoin these conjunctions — i.e., produce a disjunctive normal form (DNF) that explicitly lists the satisfying assignments. Constant-F case handled separately (eg. A1 ∧ ¬A1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disjunctive normal form existence (Corollary 15C)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any wff ϕ we can find a tautologically equivalent wff α in disjunctive normal form (DNF).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DNF is a disjunction of conjunctions of literals; it explicitly lists the truth assignments satisfying the formula. The constructive proof in Theorem 15B yields a DNF.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness of a set of connectives ({∧,∨,¬})
rubrics_metrics.description: Because every function G : {F, T}^n → {F, T} (n ≥ 1) can be realized by a wff using only ∧, ∨, ¬, the set {∧, ∨, ¬} is complete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Completeness means any Boolean function can be expressed; practically, given any ϕ, one can build a tautologically equivalent α using only those connectives (construct via DNF).

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness of {¬, ∧} and {¬, ∨} (Theorem 15D)
rubrics_metrics.description: Both {¬, ∧} and {¬, ∨} are complete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show how to eliminate ∨ using De Morgan: β ∨ γ |==| ¬(¬β ∧ ¬γ) and similarly eliminate ∧ from {¬,∨}. Proofs typically proceed by structural induction on formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method to show a set of connectives is not complete
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a set of connectives is not complete, show (usually by induction) that any formula using only those connectives has some peculiarity, and then exhibit a Boolean function lacking that peculiarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: {∧, →} is not complete because any formula using only these connectives is T when all sentence symbols are T, so there is no formula equivalent to ¬A. Use induction on formula construction to prove the preserved peculiarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification/count of n-ary connectives
rubrics_metrics.description: For each n there are 2^{2^n} n-place Boolean functions (i.e., connectives). Example: two 0-place functions, four unary, sixteen binary (but only ten 'really binary'), 256 ternary connectives with classification of how many are essentially lower-arity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this counting to identify how many distinct connective behaviors exist at each arity and to reason about which are 'really' n-ary vs essentially unary or constants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Familiar binary connectives and equivalences (table guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: List of standard binary connectives (projection, negation, ∧, ∨, →, ↔, exclusive-or +, NOR ↓, NAND |, etc.) with equivalent expressions and algebraic interpretations (e.g., ∧ gives multiplication modulo 2 if F=0,T=1; + is addition mod 2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the table to recognize when a binary connective is essentially unary or constant, and to translate between notations (e.g., Sheffer stroke | and NOR ↓ are functionally complete).

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness by single connectives or small sets (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: { | } (Sheffer stroke) is complete; {¬, →} is complete (most binary connectives together with ¬ are complete except + and ↔); {⊥, →} is 'supercomplete' since it realizes 0-place functions as well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text sketches constructions and/or references exercises showing how to simulate standard connectives using these small sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of delay (depth) of a circuit/formula
rubrics_metrics.description: Delay of a sentence symbol is 0; delay of ¬α is one greater than delay(α); delay of α ∧ β is one greater than max(delay(α), delay(β)). Similarly for other connectives. The delay of a circuit is the maximum number of boxes a signal passes through from input to output.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delay measures propagation time; circuits/formulas with equal truth-tables may differ in cost (number of devices) and delay. Optimization often trades cost vs delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circuit/formula optimization problem statement
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a circuit (or its wff) and a catalog of available devices (each corresponding to connectives), find an equivalent circuit (tautologically equivalent wff) minimizing cost subject to constraints such as a maximum allowable delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical constraints: available devices should correspond to a complete set; examples show constructing majority or equality circuits with limited device types. The problem of finding minimal-cost solutions is generally hard; examples demonstrate ad hoc simplifications (e.g., factoring to avoid duplication).

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicant and prime implicant principle for minimal DNF
rubrics_metrics.description: A literal is either a sentence symbol or its negation. An implicant of ϕ is a conjunction α of literals (using distinct sentence symbols) such that α |= ϕ. An implicant α is prime iff deleting any literal ceases to be an implicant. Any minimum-length disjunction of implicants equivalent to ϕ must consist only of prime implicants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use prime implicants to form minimal DNFs; this is the basis for simplification techniques in circuit design (e.g., Karnaugh maps, Quine–McCluskey). Exercises illustrate finding all prime implicants and forming equivalent minimal disjunctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of satisfiable set of wffs
rubrics_metrics.description: A set Γ of wffs is satisfiable iff there is a truth assignment that satisfies every member of Γ. Γ is finitely satisfiable iff every finite subset of Γ is satisfiable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These notions set up the Compactness Theorem and are used in proofs that extend finitely satisfiable sets to maximal ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compactness theorem (sentential logic)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of wffs is satisfiable iff every finite subset is satisfiable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof strategy: enumerate wffs, extend Γ recursively to a maximal finitely satisfiable set Δ with the property that for every α either α∈Δ or ¬α∈Δ, then define v(A)=T iff A∈Δ and show v satisfies exactly the formulas in Δ. Zorn's lemma provides an alternative construction when sentence symbols are uncountable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite basis for entailment (Corollary 17A)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Γ |= τ then there is a finite Γ0 ⊆ Γ such that Γ0 |= τ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a direct corollary of compactness: entailment from a (possibly infinite) set reduces to entailment from some finite subset; used in algorithms and theoretical reductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informal definition of effective procedure (algorithmic effectiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: An effective procedure must (1) have exact instructions of finite length; (2) be mechanically implementable (require no originality or randomness); (3) in decision procedures, produce a yes/no answer in a finite number of steps for each input (no bound on time/space is required a priori).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This informal notion is sufficient for positive existence proofs; precise counterparts (e.g., 'recursive') appear later. The text notes practical distinctions (reasonable time) but uses the unbounded formal notion for theoretical results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decidability of wffs (Theorem 17B) and input encoding
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an effective procedure that, given any expression ε, will decide whether or not it is a wff. To avoid infinitely many atomic symbols, use an input format like A'''... (e.g., A'''' for A5) so the alphabet reduces to a finite set of symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The algorithm follows the grammar/formation rules (see Section 1.3). The technical input alphabet consists of 9 symbols: (, ), ¬, ∧, ∨, →, ↔, A, and '.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decidability of tautological consequence for finite premises (Theorem 17C and Corollary 17D)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an effective procedure that, given a finite set Γ and τ, will decide whether Γ |= τ. In particular, for finite Γ the set of tautological consequences is decidable; the set of tautologies is decidable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the truth-table procedure. The requirement that Γ be finite is necessary because one cannot be given an infinite object directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectively enumerable / semidecidable equivalence (Theorem 17E)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set A of expressions is effectively enumerable iff there exists an effective procedure that, given any expression ε, produces the answer 'yes' iff ε ∈ A. Equivalently, A is semidecidable iff membership has a semi-decision procedure (halts and says 'yes' for members, may run forever otherwise).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: to enumerate from a semidecision procedure, dovetail checks across all expressions; conversely, to semidecide from an enumeration, watch the list until ε appears. This justifies the common interchangeable use of 'effectively enumerable' and 'semidecidable'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kleene's theorem for decidability (Theorem 17F)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of expressions is decidable iff both it and its complement are effectively enumerable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This characterizes decidable sets as those for which both membership and non-membership can be enumerated; exercise referenced for proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerability of tautological consequences for decidable premises (Theorem 17G)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Γ is a decidable (or effectively enumerable) set of wffs, then the set of tautological consequences of Γ is effectively enumerable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: enumerate Γ as σ1, σ2, ... and test by truth-tables whether ∅ |= τ, {σ1} |= τ, {σ1,σ2} |= τ, ...; by compactness, if Γ |= τ some finite subset will suffice and the procedure will eventually affirm τ. This yields an effective enumeration of consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of computable (effectively computable) function
rubrics_metrics.description: A function f is effectively computable (computable) iff there exists an effective procedure that, given an input x, will eventually produce the correct output f(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No explicit resource bounds are imposed; the notion is the algorithmic one that will be made formal (recursive) later in the book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjunctive normal form (CNF) existence (exercise statement)
rubrics_metrics.description: A formula α is in conjunctive normal form (CNF) iff it is a conjunction of disjunctions of literals; for any formula, one can find a tautologically equivalent formula in CNF.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This complements the DNF corollary and is standard: transform via logical equivalences (e.g., distribute ∧ over ∨ after moving negations inward) or use dual construction to DNF. Exercise 9 asks to exhibit CNF for A↔B↔C and to prove general existence.
